job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Victor Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Victor, and thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented room with my friend Kofi in Port Marlow, with a desk each and a kettle that never works. I start with a run, then I spend three hours on applications, but I automate half of it: a script I wrote pulls new finance jobs into a sheet, and an AI tool helps me tailor each cover letter. After lunch I do small freelance jobs, mostly cleaning up spreadsheets for a bakery and a bike shop. I did a finance degree and passed without internships, because I spent my second year building side projects. Five months after graduating I've had three interviews and no offer, which stings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a slightly overhyped tool, useful for drafts and spreadsheets but not much else. I'd tell friends to keep using it anyway, because small savings add up. Online I'd post that we still need rules on data and on how firms use these tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it changes little for me. I'm already using AI every day, so my edge is small and my real problem is a pass degree and no internships. Hype or not, the entry market is hard and I've got some debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the daily routine, add five more applications a week, and aim my freelance work at three more small businesses so I have references. I'd offer a monthly bookkeeping clean-up for a flat fee. I'd also ask my cousin in Dunmore, who works at a credit union, whether they take trainees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit impatient, not scared. I'd rather things move and I could use my skills, so a flat world is slightly annoying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think is holding back the interviews from turning into an offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three interviews all asked about internships and group projects, and I had one project on my own. The feedback was friendly, but a pass is a pass. I think a person scanning the CV stops at the grade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in your side projects that a firm could see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show a shared dashboard I built for the bakery, with sales by hour and a little forecast. The owner says it saved her two hours a week. That's the sort of thing I'd put in front of a firm to show I can finish something real.

say: I'd say AI is **overhyped** but useful for drafts and spreadsheets, so friends should keep using it.
Online I'd push for **rules** on data and how firms use these tools.
think: It changes little for me, since I already use AI daily and my **edge** is small.
My real problem is a **pass degree** and no internships.
do: Add **five more** applications a week and pitch three more small businesses for freelance work.
Offer a flat-fee **bookkeeping** clean-up and ask my cousin at a credit union about trainees.
feel: **Impatient**, not scared, because a flat world wastes my skills.
S0.quote: Hype or not, the entry market is hard and I've got some debt.
fieldNote: He is **uneasy** about the grade and debt, not about AI, since he already works with it.
His freelance proof, the bakery dashboard, is a real asset.
Impatience, not fear, shows his adaptive style.

steps.text: Send five more applications a week on top of the current routine
Offer small shops a monthly bookkeeping clean-up for a flat fee
Ask my cousin whether the credit union takes trainees
Build a sales dashboard for the bike shop as a second reference

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the interesting part is who gets help. Some people will use the tools and double their output, and others will get left behind. I'd argue for public training, easy access to the tools and unions for young workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my position is better than most juniors. I can build the checks and automations that firms now buy. But the entry jobs I'm applying for are exactly the ones that disappear when two people do the work of five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go bigger on the freelance side: automations for payroll and invoice checks for small businesses, charged per month. I'd learn a proper data language, say Python, through a cheap evening course. I'd apply to roles that mention analyst or operations, not just accounting, and I'd put a part of every client payment aside as a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and slightly nervous. It's like watching a wave and knowing I can ride it if I get up early enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you think your own skills sit when software takes over the checking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the work I like is the thinking about what to check. Software does the checking, but someone has to design it and explain why a number looks wrong. That's where I want to sit, between the data and the owner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell Kofi if you had to change direction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, mate, I'm moving to analyst work or going fully independent. Kofi would roll his eyes and say he knew it. Then we'd probably split the rent differently, because he works nights.

say: I'd say the question is who gets **help**: some double their output, others fall behind.
I'd argue for public training and easy access to **tools**.
think: My position is better than most juniors because I can **build** the checks firms now buy.
Entry jobs like mine **disappear** when two people do the work of five.
do: Sell **monthly** automations for payroll and invoice checks to small businesses.
Learn **Python** in a cheap evening course and apply to analyst and operations roles.
feel: **Excited** and slightly nervous, like watching a wave I can ride if I rise early.
S1.quote: Software does the checking, but someone has to design it and explain why a number looks wrong.
fieldNote: He sees himself as **exposed and ready**: the job he applies for shrinks, the skill he builds grows.
He puts part of each client payment aside, which shows realism.
Excitement is real, but he still has no offer.

steps.text: Sell monthly payroll and invoice-check automations to small businesses
Take an evening Python course
Apply to analyst and operations roles as well as accounting
Set aside a fifth of every client payment as a cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to move faster than any government has moved before. I'd want income support, a public stake in the gains and some form of notice period. I'd say it loudly, online and at any meeting I can find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm unsettled. I'm not afraid of the tools, but if AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, then my freelance edge disappears too. I'd be competing against the tool itself, and a pass degree wouldn't matter either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pivot hard to things that need a person physically present or legally accountable, like running books for tiny businesses with a face-to-face relationship. I'd cut spending to the bone, ask my parents for a loan if needed, and get any job with a regulated licence. I'd also join a group fighting for a share of AI gains, because that matters as much as skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed but alive. It feels dizzy, like standing at the top of a slide, but I'd still do something with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If thinking work is cheap by 2028, what is left for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone who sold this as free progress without a plan. Companies, and yes governments who treated it as a debate topic. I'd be angry at myself too for learning the tools instead of asking who would own them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you angry at, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The pay thing is real. If the tools do the work and the owners keep all the money, no amount of skill saves us. That's why I'd put time into the political side, not only my CV.

say: I'd say we must move faster than any government has before, with **income support** and a public stake.
I'd say it loudly, online and at any **meeting**.
think: If AI does any thinking work better and cheaper, my **freelance edge** vanishes too.
I'd be competing against the **tool** itself.
do: Pivot to **face-to-face** bookkeeping for tiny businesses, where a person is accountable.
Cut spending, borrow from my parents if needed and join a group fighting for a **share** of the gains.
feel: **Alarmed** but alive, like standing at the top of a slide.
S2.quote: If the tools do the work and the owners keep all the money, no amount of skill saves us.
fieldNote: Even his strong **AI skills** do not protect him if AI itself becomes the competitor.
He moves quickly toward politics, which fits his progressive view.
His mood stays anxious, not alarmed, because he has options and family backing.

steps.text: Pivot to face-to-face bookkeeping for tiny local businesses
Cut spending to rent, food and loan payments only
Join a group fighting for a public share of AI gains
Ask my parents for a loan if work dries up

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something, so let's build it properly. I'd press for public training and a fair share of the gains, and I'd show people how to use the tools now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel cautious. I can see myself with a first job, a decent record and a freelance base by then. I'd still be unsure what remains after 2031, but I'd have options, and that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd take any analyst or finance operations job to get a reference and a salary, even if it's below my skills. I'd keep two freelance clients on the side. I'd also save at least a third of my income and learn one new thing each quarter, like data pipelines or compliance basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cautiously optimistic. I'd say it feels like an exam with a long revision period.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different for you than two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is a sprint where you can't plan. Five years is a plan with room for mistakes. I can try a path, change it and still have time left.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably keep Kofi as a flatmate and save for a deposit later. A small thing, but life goes on and I'd want to keep the normal parts.

say: I'd say five years is enough to **build** properly, with training and a fair share of the gains.
I'd show people how to use the **tools** now.
think: I feel cautious: I can see a first job and **freelance** base by then.
I'm unsure what remains after 2031, but **options** matter.
do: Take any analyst job for a **reference** and salary and keep two freelance clients.
Save a **third** of my income and learn one new thing each quarter.
feel: Cautiously **optimistic**, like an exam with long revision time.
S3.quote: Two years is a sprint where you can't plan. Five years is a plan with room for mistakes.
fieldNote: The longer **runway** shifts him from anxious to uneasy.
He plans a mix: salary, freelance, savings and learning.
Normal life, a flatshare and a deposit, still matters to him.

steps.text: Take the first analyst or finance operations job offered
Keep two freelance clients alongside the job
Save a third of every month's income
Learn one new skill each quarter, starting with data pipelines

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to get this right, so let's set up the rules, the training and the sharing of gains while we can. I'd tell friends to stay curious and to push their employers on how they use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly calm. Ten years is enough to build a track record, change field if needed and maybe start a small company. I'd see the change as a tide to ride, not a wall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first decent job, then use evenings to build a small tool, maybe a bookkeeping assistant for tiny firms. If it works I'd turn it into a business by year three. I'd save for a flat, learn about regulation, and keep my AI skills sharp because that's the fastest-changing part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Light, almost excited. There's room to try things and fail once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does ten years make you want to do something bigger?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. I'd like to build a product, not just sell my hours. With ten years, I could try that and still have a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about how you use the next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Be less casual about proof. Make every project a small case study with numbers, so the next interviewer has something to hold. That's the simple lesson from three interviews.

say: I'd say we have **time** to set rules, training and gain-sharing while we can.
I'd tell friends to stay **curious** and press their employers.
think: I'm fairly **calm**: ten years is enough to build a track record or a small company.
I see the change as a **tide** to ride, not a wall.
do: Take a decent first job, then build a **bookkeeping assistant** in the evenings.
Save for a **flat**, study regulation and keep my AI skills sharp.
feel: **Light**, almost excited, with room to try and fail once.
S4.quote: I'd see the change as a tide to ride, not a wall.
fieldNote: His **adaptive** style and a decade of warning combine to make him calm.
He wants a product, not only paid hours.
Proof through small case studies is his practical lesson from the job hunt.

steps.text: Take the first decent finance or analyst job offered
Build a bookkeeping assistant tool for tiny firms in the evenings
Save steadily for a flat deposit
Keep up with each new AI tool and write up the results

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most. It leaves no time to build a track record, and even my AI skills might not matter. What would help is a public share of the gains, a safety net while people retrain, and a real way for young people to get a first job. A mentor wouldn't hurt either.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people say my generation is lucky because we can use the tools. Using them is easy. Owning anything because of them is the hard part.

headlineQuote: Using them is easy. Owning anything because of them is the hard part.
portrait: Victor is a 23-year-old finance graduate who shares a rented room in **Port Marlow** and uses AI every day.
He passed without internships, has **no offer** after three interviews and earns from small freelance spreadsheet jobs.
He is progressive and adaptive: he wants public **training and a share** of the gains.
He stays uneasy or calm in most pictures and becomes **anxious** only when AI itself is the competitor.
He sees himself as the person who designs checks, not just does them.
biggestWorry: He worries most about **AGI by 2028**, because even his strong AI skills may not be worth anything.
whatWouldHelp: A public **share** of the gains and a safety net while people retrain.
A real route for young people into a **first job**.
